title: Turnkey hotel and aparthotel FF&E: rooms, lobby, bathrooms
seo_title: Hotel FF&E Procurement Turnkey: Rooms, Lobby, Baths
description: Turnkey FF&E for a hotel or aparthotel: a mock-up room, bathrooms, lobby, textiles, 30–60 day delivery from China, ready-made kits and a budget benchmark.
lead: Furnishing a hotel or aparthotel means buying dozens of identical items that have to survive guests, housekeeping and suitcases every single day. Here is where to start, how an aparthotel differs from a classic hotel, how not to miss the opening date and how to use ready-made kits as a starting specification.

body: h2
What hotel FF&E includes
p

A hotel consists of several types of space, and each needs its own specification. Guest rooms are replicated dozens of times, the lobby is the hotel's calling card, bathrooms must be practical and easy to clean, and textiles and consumables are needed with a reserve for changeovers between guests.
ul
guest rooms: beds, bedside tables, wardrobes, desk, armchairs, lighting, curtains
bathrooms: sanitary ware, backlit mirrors, wet-area light fittings, accessories
lobby and reception: lounge furniture, side tables, decorative lighting, rugs, decor
breakfast area or restaurant: tables, chairs, tableware
corridors and stairs: wayfinding and decorative lighting, floor finishes
textiles: bed linen, towels, bathrobes, bedspreads, throws
p

Good FF&E starts not with a catalogue but with a concept: who the hotel is for, the average length of stay, what a guest should feel in the room. That determines materials, furniture level and budget.
h2
The mock-up room: test before you replicate
p

A mistake in one room multiplies across the whole hotel. That is why we recommend assembling a mock-up room first: bed, bedside tables, reading lights, wardrobe, desk, curtains and a bathroom with every accessory. It is used to test guest scenarios: is there room to open a suitcase, are there enough sockets by the bed and desk, does the light dazzle, is it easy to clean under the bed and in the shower?
p

After testing, the specification is adjusted and only then ordered for every room. A small inconvenience — a wall light without its own switch or a hook at the wrong height — then does not turn into hundreds of complaints in reviews.

h2
Aparthotels: how the furnishing differs
p

In an aparthotel guests stay longer, and an apartment is closer to a home than to a hotel room. Besides the bedroom and bathroom you need a kitchen or kitchenette, a dining area, more storage and a washing machine or laundry access. The interior should feel homely and cosy, yet withstand hotel-level guest turnover.
ul
kitchen module with sink, tap and storage
dining table for 2–4 and easy-to-clean chairs
wardrobe and storage for longer stays
cookware and tableware for each apartment
textiles with a reserve: two or three sets per apartment
p

In an aparthotel it is especially important that all units of one type are identical: cleaning, restocking and repairs become much simpler. Different unit types — studios, one- and two-bedroom apartments — get their own specifications based on a shared palette and materials.
h2
Requirements for furniture and materials
p

Hotel furniture works far harder than residential furniture. So construction matters as much as looks: bed frames, hardware fixings, surfaces resistant to moisture and cleaning products, removable covers on upholstery. Specific material requirements are defined for each property and hotel format.
ul
surfaces that are easy to wipe and fabrics that withstand frequent cleaning
light fittings that are easy to reach for lamp changes and maintenance
ranges that can be reordered a year or two later
sanitary ware and accessories from one collection for all bathrooms

h2
Lobby, reception and corridors
p

The lobby creates the first impression before check-in. This is the place for the strongest accents: lounge seating, decorative lighting, a fireplace, rugs, plants and art. The reception desk is usually made to measure, while the rest can be assembled from ready-made items. Corridors are often underestimated, though guests walk them every day: calm lighting, quiet flooring and clear wayfinding to the rooms matter here.
p
Design the lobby around real scenarios: where guests wait for check-in with luggage, where they work on a laptop, where they meet friends. Each scenario needs its own furniture and lighting.
h2
Breakfast area, restaurant and terrace
p

Even a small hotel usually has a place where guests have breakfast or spend the evening. The same rules apply as in a restaurant: sturdy chairs, tables that can be rearranged for groups, lighting that changes from morning to evening, and tableware from one range that can be reordered. If there is a terrace or courtyard, outdoor furniture is chosen in aluminium, teak and outdoor fabrics, with heaters and lighting for cool evenings.
h2
Textiles and consumables: how much to plan
p

Textiles are the item most often estimated by eye and then bought in a hurry. Bed linen, towels and bathrobes are needed not as one set per room but with a reserve: one set in the room, one in the laundry and one as a replacement for worn items. The same goes for kitchenware in apartments and tableware in the breakfast area. It is better to choose a range you can reorder than to hunt for a similar shade a year later.
h2
Ready-made kits as a starting specification
p

So you do not have to build the specification from scratch, we have prepared [ready-made project kits (in Ukrainian)](/ozdoba/komplekty) from our Ozdoba catalogue. Each kit is priced as the sum of its catalogue items, and its contents and quantities are adjusted to your hotel. For hotels and aparthotels the following work well:
ul
Hotel rooms ×10 — bedroom, workspace and bathroom for ten rooms
Aparthotel bathrooms ×8 — wall-hung frames, vanities, mirrors, shower systems, porcelain tiles
Mini-hotel lobby and reception — lounge area, fireplace, floor lamps, rugs and decor
p

Kit prices are indicative: your manager confirms the final cost, availability and delivery time after your enquiry. The minimum order starts at $500; invoices are issued for companies registered in Ukraine, and EU invoicing is coming soon.
h2
Who decides and how approvals work
p

In a hotel project decisions are often made by several people: owner, general manager, operator, investor. To keep approvals from dragging on for weeks, we put the specification into one table with photos, dimensions, colours and prices, and show key items as physical samples. Every change is logged, so at the end there is no question about who replaced a fabric or a light fitting and when.
h2
Timing: how not to miss the opening date
p

Delivery from China takes 30–60 days. If furniture is ordered after the renovation is finished, the hotel stands empty while the shipment is on its way. So we approve the specification during rough works and place orders so that everything arrives before final finishing. Before a shipment leaves we check it is complete, and after delivery we assemble, place everything and hand over rooms ready for guests.

h2
Budget: a benchmark at our rates
p

A hotel budget consists of the design project, renovation and FF&E. For a 600 m² aparthotel a benchmark at our rates is: interior design from $30 × 600 m² = from $18,000; renovation from $550 × 600 m² = from $330,000. FF&E is calculated from the specification, and the ready-made kits above give a sense of the order of magnitude. The exact figure comes from the estimate for your project, and if CAS carries out the renovation we keep the final cost within ±5% of the estimate.
